description:
Did You Know You Traveled 940 Million km This Year?

Episode 52 of a daily journey through the universe. 🎆
Happy New Year! In one year Earth travels about 940 million kilometers around the Sun at about 30 km per second. And tomorrow evening (January 2) Earth reaches perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in the middle of northern winter.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 53: Next stop, the Quadrantids. The first meteor shower of the year, peaking the night of January 3 to 4.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

Images: NASA (public domain)
Narration: AI voice

#space #newyear #astronomy #shorts #science

segments.text: You traveled nine hundred and forty million kilometers this year, without leaving home. Here's how.
Last night, a new year began. Since last January, you've ridden Earth all the way around the Sun, one more time.
segments.headline: Another lap complete

segments.text: In one year, Earth travels about nine hundred forty million kilometers.
That's about thirty kilometers every second. More than a hundred thousand kilometers per hour.
And you didn't feel a thing, because everything around you, the air, the oceans, is moving with you.
segments.headline: You didn't feel it

segments.text: Here's a surprise. Tomorrow evening, January second, Earth reaches its closest point to the Sun all year. It's called perihelion.
segments.headline: Closest to the Sun

segments.text: Earth will be about one hundred forty-seven million kilometers away. In July, it's about five million kilometers farther.
So why is it winter in the north? Because seasons don't come from distance. They come from Earth's tilt.
segments.headline: Seasons come from the tilt

segments.text: Right now the north is tilted away from the Sun, so sunlight is weaker. In Australia and Argentina, it's summer.
segments.headline: Summer down south

segments.text: A new lap begins right now. Happy twenty twenty-seven, from Next Stop Universe.
Tomorrow, the first shooting stars of the year. Next stop: the Quadrantids. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
